q: Before you move off from the side of the road, what should you do?
e: Use your mirrors, look round to check your blind spot, and signal if it would help other road users.
o: Check your mirrors and blind spot, then signal if necessary
Signal and move off straight away
Sound your horn and move off
Look only in your interior mirror

q: What is a "blind spot"?
e: Blind spots are areas your mirrors don't show. Look over your shoulder to check them.
o: An area around your vehicle you can't see in your mirrors
An area lit only by your headlights
The part of the road in front of the bonnet
A dark patch on the road at night

q: When should you check your mirrors?
e: Mirror – signal – manoeuvre: always check your mirrors before signalling, turning or slowing down.
o: Before signalling, changing direction or changing speed
Only when you are about to stop

q: What does the routine "Mirror – Signal – Manoeuvre" (MSM) help you do?
e: MSM makes sure you know what is around you before you act, and lets others know your plans.

q: You are driving and feel tired. What should you do?
e: The Highway Code says to stop somewhere safe, drink two cups of a caffeinated drink and take a short nap of at least 15 minutes.
o: Stop at a safe place, take a short nap and have two caffeinated drinks
Open the window and keep going
Drive faster to finish the journey sooner

q: How often should you take a break on a long journey?
e: Plan your journey to take breaks of at least 15 minutes every two hours.
o: At least 15 minutes every two hours

q: You must not stop on the hard shoulder of a motorway to rest if you feel tired.
e: True — leave at the next exit or services. The hard shoulder is for emergencies only.

q: When is it legal to use a hand-held mobile phone while driving?
e: It's illegal to hold a phone while driving, including when stopped in traffic or at lights. Only use it when safely parked.
o: When you are stopped in a traffic jam
When you are at traffic lights

q: What is the penalty for using a hand-held phone while driving?
e: Using a hand-held phone while driving can get you 6 penalty points and a £200 fine.

q: Using a hands-free phone can still distract you, and you can be prosecuted if you are not in proper control.
e: True — hands-free is legal, but it can still distract you. The police can still stop you.

q: You are driving and your phone rings. What should you do?
e: Keep your attention on driving. Find a safe place to stop before using your phone.
o: Let it go to voicemail and return the call when safely parked
Pull onto the hard shoulder to answer
Answer it on speaker while holding it

q: Which of these can distract you while driving?
e: Set your sat nav before you set off. Don't let it distract you while driving.
o: Using a sat nav while moving

q: You are approaching a bend. Your view ahead is blocked. What should you do?
e: Drive at a speed that lets you stop within the distance you can see to be clear.
o: Slow down and be ready to stop
Sound your horn and keep going
Speed up to get round quickly
Move to the middle of the road

q: You are about to turn right into a side road. What should you check just before you turn?
e: Check your mirrors and right blind spot — motorcyclists or cyclists may be overtaking you.
o: Your right mirror and blind spot, for overtaking vehicles such as motorcyclists

q: What should you do before reversing?
e: Check all around before and while reversing. Small children may be hard to see.
o: Look all around, including behind you, for pedestrians and other road users
Sound your horn and reverse quickly

q: You are reversing. Who should you be most careful of?
e: Small children can be hidden behind your vehicle. Look carefully all round, and get help if you can't see.
o: Small children, who may be hidden from view
Cyclists on the other side of the road

q: When are you most likely to lose concentration?
e: Long, monotonous drives can make you lose concentration. Take regular breaks.
o: On long, boring journeys such as motorways
When you have just set off

q: A driver flashes their headlights at you. What does it mean, according to the Highway Code?
e: Only flash your headlights to let others know you are there. Never assume it means "go ahead".
o: They are letting you know they are there
You must give way to them

q: When is it safe to emerge from a junction where your view is blocked?
e: Edge forward slowly until you can see properly. Don't rely on hearing.
o: When you have crept forward slowly until you can see clearly
When you have sounded your horn
As soon as there is a gap in traffic you can hear

q: Which of these is the safest way to use a sat nav?
e: Plan your route before you set off.
o: Set it before your journey and only glance at it
Watch it instead of the road

q: You should only use your horn while moving, to warn others of your presence.
e: True — don't use it aggressively. Don't sound it in a built-up area between 11.30pm and 7am unless another vehicle poses a danger.

q: Between what times must you not use your horn in a built-up area, unless a moving vehicle poses a danger?
e: Don't use your horn in a built-up area between 11.30pm and 7am, or when stationary, unless a moving vehicle poses a danger.

q: Why should you look well ahead when driving?
e: Looking well ahead gives you time to plan and react to hazards.
o: To spot hazards early and have time to react
To read signs further away only

q: Your vision is blurred on a long drive because you are tired. What is most important?
e: If you feel tired or your vision is affected, stop and rest.
o: Open a window and drive faster

q: You are waiting to emerge at a junction. The windscreen pillar is blocking your view. What should you watch out for?
e: Windscreen pillars can hide motorcyclists and cyclists. Move your head to check.
o: Motorcyclists and cyclists hidden behind the pillar

q: Another driver is tailgating you (driving too close behind). What should you do?
e: Leave more room in front, so you can slow down gently if you need to. Don't brake sharply.
o: Gradually increase the gap in front of you

q: What is the two-second rule?
e: Leave at least a two-second gap in good conditions. Double it on wet roads.
o: Keeping at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle in front in good conditions
Waiting two seconds at give way lines

q: In wet weather, what gap should you leave behind the vehicle in front?
e: Wet roads at least double your stopping distance, so leave at least a four-second gap.

q: You are following a slow-moving vehicle on a narrow road. What should you do?
e: Be patient and only overtake when it's safe and legal.
o: Stay back until you can overtake safely
Overtake on a bend to save time

q: A driver pulls out in front of you at a junction. What should you do?
e: Don't react aggressively. Stay calm and keep a safe distance.
o: Flash your headlights and sound your horn
Overtake them as soon as possible

q: At a zebra crossing, a pedestrian has stepped onto the crossing. What must you do?
e: You MUST give way when a pedestrian has moved onto a zebra crossing.
o: Give way and let them cross

q: At a zebra crossing, a pedestrian is waiting to cross. What should you do?
e: Give way to pedestrians waiting to cross a zebra crossing. Don't wave them across — another vehicle may not stop.
o: Be ready to slow down and stop to let them cross
Sound your horn to hurry them
Speed up to pass before they step out

q: Why should you never wave people across at pedestrian crossings?
e: Waving could lead someone into danger from other traffic.
o: There may be another vehicle coming that won't stop
It's against the law to wave

q: A bus is signalling to pull out from a bus stop ahead. What should you do?
e: Give way to buses signalling to pull away from stops, if it is safe.
o: Give way to it if it is safe to do so
Flash your lights to make it wait

q: An emergency vehicle with flashing blue lights is behind you. What should you do?
e: Help it pass safely, without breaking the law or putting others at risk. Don't mount the kerb dangerously or go through red lights.
o: Pull over where it is safe and legal to let it pass
Drive through a red light to get out of its way

q: A vehicle with flashing green lights is behind you. Who could it be?
e: Doctors may use flashing green beacons when answering an emergency call.
o: A doctor on an emergency call

q: Which vehicle uses flashing amber beacons?
e: Flashing amber beacons warn of slow-moving or large vehicles.
o: A slow-moving or wide vehicle, such as a road gritter or tractor

q: Another driver makes a mistake. How should you react?
e: Be patient. Everyone makes mistakes.
o: Stay calm and don't take it personally
Flash your lights and gesture at them
Overtake them to show your anger

q: You are in a queue of traffic. A driver wants to pull out of a side road. What should you do?
e: Be considerate. Letting others out keeps traffic flowing.
o: Let them out if it's safe and you won't block anything
Move forward to close the gap

q: You are in a slow queue. A motorcyclist is filtering between lanes. What should you do?
e: Motorcyclists may filter. Check mirrors and blind spots before changing lanes.
o: Check your mirrors and be careful before changing lanes or opening doors
Open your door to warn them

q: Which of these is the most likely to make you drive too fast?
e: Don't let time pressure affect your driving. It's better to arrive late than not at all.

q: You may overtake a vehicle that has stopped to let pedestrians cross at a crossing.
e: False — you MUST NOT overtake the vehicle nearest a crossing, or one that has stopped to give way to pedestrians.

q: When should you use hazard warning lights?
e: Use them when stationary to warn you are obstructing traffic. On a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway, you may use them briefly to warn of a hazard ahead.
o: When you are stopped and temporarily obstructing traffic

q: When should you sound your horn?
e: Only use the horn to warn others of your presence.
o: To warn others of your presence
To hurry up a slow driver

q: A learner driver stalls at traffic lights in front of you. What should you do?
e: Learners may make mistakes. Give them time.

q: You are behind an older driver who is driving slowly. What should you do?
e: Older drivers may be slower to react. Be patient.
o: Be patient and allow them extra time

q: Coming towards you is a large vehicle on a narrow road. What should you do?
e: Be prepared to give way on narrow roads.
o: Slow down and be ready to stop or pull into a passing place

q: What should you use a passing place on a single-track road for?
e: Pull into a passing place on your left, or wait opposite one on your right. Don't park in them.
o: To let oncoming traffic pass, or to let traffic behind overtake

q: In a traffic queue, you should leave junctions clear so other traffic can get in and out.
e: True — don't block junctions, even in slow traffic.

q: You are following a cyclist. You want to turn left just ahead. What should you do?
e: Don't cut across cyclists going ahead when you turn. Wait behind them.
o: Stay behind them and let them pass the junction before you turn
Overtake and turn left in front of them
Sound your horn so they move over

q: What is the legal minimum tread depth for car tyres?
e: Car tyres must have at least 1.6 mm of tread across the central three-quarters, around the entire tyre.
o: 1.6 mm across the central three-quarters of the tread, all the way round

q: When should you check your tyre pressures?
e: Check pressures when tyres are cold, using the figures in your vehicle handbook.
o: When the tyres are cold, before a journey
Only when the warning light comes on

q: What can under-inflated tyres cause?
e: Wrong tyre pressures affect braking, steering and fuel use.
o: Worse fuel economy, heavier steering and longer stopping distances

q: Your car pulls to one side when you brake. What is the most likely cause?
e: Have your brakes checked by a qualified mechanic as soon as possible.
o: The brakes need adjusting or repairing

q: Your brake pedal feels spongy. What should you do?
e: A spongy pedal can mean air in the brake system or low fluid — get it checked straight away.
o: Have the brakes checked before driving any further
Pump the pedal and carry on

q: A warning light shows on your dashboard while driving. What should you do?
e: Know your warning lights. Red usually means stop safely as soon as possible.
o: Check what it means in your vehicle handbook and act on it
Ignore it if the car feels fine
Turn the engine off immediately on the motorway

q: Why should you keep your windscreen, windows and lights clean?
e: Dirty windows and lights reduce visibility, especially at night and in bad weather.
o: So you can see and be seen clearly

q: It is illegal to drive with a windscreen, windows or mirrors that you can't see through clearly.
e: True — all windows must be clear of ice, snow, condensation and dirt before you drive.

q: What should you do before driving in frosty weather?
e: You must be able to see clearly in all directions.
o: Clear all ice and snow from windows, lights, mirrors and number plates
Clear just a small hole in the windscreen
Drive off and let the heater clear it
Use the wipers on dry ice

q: What is the main reason for having correctly adjusted head restraints?
e: Adjust the head restraint so the rigid part is at least as high as your eyes or the top of your ears, and as close to the back of your head as is comfortable.
o: To reduce the risk of neck injury in a collision

q: Who is responsible for making sure children under 14 wear a seat belt or use a suitable child restraint?
e: The driver is legally responsible for passengers under 14.
o: The child's parent, even if not in the car

q: Who is responsible for wearing a seat belt if a passenger is 14 or over?
e: Passengers aged 14 and over are responsible for wearing their own seat belt.

q: Up to what height or age must children normally use a child restraint?
e: Children must use the right child restraint until they are 12 or 135 cm tall, whichever comes first.
o: Until they are 12 years old or 135 cm tall, whichever comes first

q: You must never put a rear-facing baby seat in front of an active frontal airbag.
e: True — the airbag could seriously injure or kill the baby.

q: Which of these makes your car more fuel-efficient?
e: Correct tyre pressures, less weight and no roof rack all help you save fuel.
o: Keeping tyres at the correct pressure
Carrying unnecessary weight in the boot

q: How can you drive in an environmentally friendly way?
e: Smooth driving saves fuel and reduces emissions.
o: Drive smoothly, plan ahead and avoid harsh braking and acceleration
Leave the engine running when parked
Use the air conditioning all the time

q: You are stopped in traffic for some time. What can you do to reduce pollution?
e: The Highway Code says don't leave your engine running unnecessarily while stationary.
o: Switch the engine off if it is safe
Rev the engine to keep it warm
Keep the lights on full beam

q: Why should you get rid of used engine oil properly?
e: Take it to a local authority site or garage. Never pour it down a drain.
o: It is harmful to the environment
It can be reused in the car
It's a fire risk at home only

q: What is the purpose of a catalytic converter?
e: A catalytic converter reduces the toxic gases from the exhaust.

q: What should you do if your vehicle's exhaust is producing a lot of smoke?
e: Excess smoke can mean an engine fault and adds to pollution.

q: When driving, where should you hold the steering wheel?
e: Keep both hands on the wheel unless you are using other controls.
o: With both hands, in a comfortable position, unless changing gear or using controls
At the bottom with one hand
At the top with one hand

q: Why should you not rest your foot on the clutch pedal while driving?
e: "Riding the clutch" wears it out and can reduce control.
o: It causes wear and reduces control
It's needed to keep the engine running

q: What is "coasting"?
e: Coasting reduces your control, especially downhill and on bends.
o: Driving with the clutch pressed down or in neutral

q: How often should you check your engine oil level?
e: Check oil, water, lights and tyres regularly and before long journeys.
o: Regularly, and before a long journey
Only when a warning light shows

q: Which of these will make a car harder to steer?
e: Low tyre pressure makes steering heavier.

q: What does a suspension fault cause?
e: Worn suspension affects control. Have it checked.

q: What is the safest way to carry a dog in a car?
e: Make sure animals are suitably restrained so they can't distract you or be hurt.
o: Restrained, for example in a dog cage, harness or guard
On a passenger's lap in the front
With its head out of the window

q: Why should you park in a well-lit area at night?
e: Lock your vehicle, remove valuables and park somewhere well lit.
o: To help stop your vehicle being broken into or stolen

q: You should never leave the keys in the ignition when you leave your car, even for a moment.
e: True — always remove the keys and lock your vehicle.

q: Your vehicle has been damaged in a crash. What should you check before driving it again?
e: Damage you can't see may affect brakes, steering or tyres.
o: That it's safe and roadworthy — get it checked by a garage if unsure

q: Which part of the car gives you the best view of the road behind?
e: Use the interior mirror first, then the door mirrors.

q: Why should you adjust your seat before driving?
e: Make sure you can reach all controls and see well.
o: So you can reach all the controls comfortably and see clearly
So the passenger has more room

q: What is the overall stopping distance at 30 mph in good conditions?
e: At 30 mph: 9 m thinking + 14 m braking = 23 m (about 6 car lengths).

q: What is the overall stopping distance at 20 mph in good conditions?
e: At 20 mph: 6 m thinking + 6 m braking = 12 m (about 3 car lengths).

q: What is the overall stopping distance at 40 mph in good conditions?
e: At 40 mph: 12 m thinking + 24 m braking = 36 m (about 9 car lengths).

q: What is the overall stopping distance at 50 mph in good conditions?
e: At 50 mph: 15 m thinking + 38 m braking = 53 m (about 13 car lengths).

q: What is the overall stopping distance at 60 mph in good conditions?
e: At 60 mph: 18 m thinking + 55 m braking = 73 m (about 18 car lengths).

q: What is the overall stopping distance at 70 mph in good conditions?
e: At 70 mph: 21 m thinking + 75 m braking = 96 m (about 24 car lengths).

q: What is the thinking distance at 30 mph?
e: Thinking distance at 30 mph is 9 metres. Braking distance is 14 metres.

q: What is the braking distance at 70 mph in good conditions?
e: Braking distance at 70 mph is 75 metres. Add 21 metres thinking distance for 96 metres overall.

q: Overall stopping distance is made up of which two parts?
e: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

q: How much longer can stopping distances be on wet roads?
e: Stopping distances are at least double in wet weather.

q: How much longer can stopping distances be on icy roads?
e: In icy conditions, braking distance can be ten times greater than on a dry road.

q: Which of these can make your thinking distance longer?
e: Tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distractions all slow your reactions.
o: Being tired, or having drunk alcohol

q: What should you do when driving in heavy rain?
e: Visibility and grip are reduced. Slow down and leave at least double the gap.
o: Slow down and leave a bigger gap
Drive closer to the car in front to follow its tyre tracks

q: Your steering suddenly feels very light in heavy rain. What is happening?
e: Ease off the accelerator and slow down gradually until the tyres grip again.
o: Your tyres are aquaplaning (losing contact with the road)

q: You are driving in snow. What should you do?
e: Use gentle controls and high gears to avoid wheelspin. Leave a big gap.
o: Drive slowly, in as high a gear as possible, and brake gently
Drive in a low gear with high revs
Brake hard if you need to stop
Keep close to the car in front

q: How should you drive on icy roads?
e: Gentle, smooth control helps avoid skidding.
o: Slowly and gently, avoiding harsh braking, steering and acceleration
In a low gear with heavy acceleration

q: What should you do if your car starts to skid?
e: If the rear skids to the right, steer to the right to recover. Don't brake harshly.
o: Ease off the accelerator and steer smoothly in the same direction as the skid
Steer the opposite way to the skid

q: What does ABS (anti-lock braking) help you do?
e: ABS stops the wheels locking so you can still steer. It doesn't always shorten stopping distances, especially on loose or wet surfaces.
o: Always stop in a shorter distance

q: Anti-lock brakes (ABS) mean you can drive faster in bad weather.
e: False — ABS helps you steer while braking, but you still need to slow down in bad weather.

q: When should you use your headlights in fog?
e: Use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced. You may also use fog lights.
o: When visibility is seriously reduced, generally to less than 100 metres

q: When must you switch off your fog lights?
e: Fog lights can dazzle others and hide your brake lights. Turn them off when visibility improves.

q: You are driving through a flood. What should you do?
e: Drive slowly with high revs to stop water getting into the exhaust. Test your brakes when you get out.
o: Drive slowly in first gear, keeping engine speed high, and test your brakes afterwards
Drive through as quickly as possible
Switch the engine off and coast

q: After driving through deep water, what should you do?
e: Brakes may not work well when wet. Test them gently at a safe place.

q: In windy weather, which road users are most likely to be blown off course?
e: Give these road users extra room in strong winds.
o: Cyclists, motorcyclists, high-sided vehicles and vehicles towing caravans

q: You are driving in very hot weather. What should you be aware of?
e: Hot weather can soften tar. Keep well ventilated so you don't get drowsy.
o: The road surface may become soft and slippery
Your tyres will have more grip

q: You are driving downhill. How can you control your speed?
e: A lower gear uses engine braking and stops your brakes overheating.
o: Select a lower gear and use the brakes gently

q: You are following a large vehicle. Why should you keep well back?
e: Dropping back helps you see past it and helps the driver see you in their mirrors.
o: To get a better view of the road ahead
So you can overtake it more easily on the left
So it can see you better in its interior mirror

q: Why should you take extra care on a bend?
e: Slow down before the bend, not on it.
o: You can't see what is round it and your vehicle may skid
You can always overtake on bends

q: When is the best time to brake for a bend?
e: Brake before the bend, when the vehicle is upright and straight.
o: Before you reach the bend, while travelling in a straight line
In the middle of the bend

q: You are driving at night with full beam on. A vehicle is coming towards you. What should you do?
e: Dip your lights so you don't dazzle oncoming drivers.

q: You are dazzled by oncoming headlights at night. What should you do?
e: Slow down or stop if dazzled, until your eyes recover.

q: In fog, why should you not follow closely behind another vehicle's rear lights?
e: Leave a big gap so you can stop in time.
o: It gives a false sense of security and you may be too close to stop

q: What is the safest gap to leave when you stop behind another vehicle in a queue?
e: This gives you room to move around it if it breaks down.
o: Enough to see its tyres touching the road

q: In icy weather, you should drive in as high a gear as possible to help prevent wheelspin.
e: True — use high gears, gentle acceleration and gentle braking.

q: On a frosty morning, where is ice likely to remain longest?
e: Bridges and shaded areas often stay icy longer.
o: In shaded areas, under trees and on bridges
At the top of hills in the sun

q: What is a "developing hazard"?
e: For example, a pedestrian who may step out, or a car pulling out.
o: Something that may make you change speed or direction
A parked car that never moves
A bend in a quiet road

q: A ball bounces into the road ahead. What should you expect?
e: Slow down and be ready to stop — a child may follow.

q: You see an ice cream van stopped ahead. What should you do?
e: Children may cross without looking. Be ready to stop.
o: Slow down — children may run out from behind it

q: You are driving past a line of parked cars. What should you watch out for?
e: Leave room for a door opening, and look for people between parked cars.
o: Pedestrians stepping out and doors opening

q: A bus has stopped at a bus stop ahead. What should you watch for?
e: People getting off a bus may cross in front of it.
o: Pedestrians coming from in front of the bus

q: You see a "school" warning sign and children near the road. What should you do?
e: Children can be unpredictable. Drive slowly.
o: Slow down and be ready to stop
Keep to the speed limit and drive on

q: What does a school crossing patrol showing a "Stop for children" sign mean?
e: You MUST stop when a school crossing patrol shows a stop sign.
o: You should give way only if children are crossing

q: You are approaching a junction. A car on the side road is edging forward. What should you do?
e: The driver may pull out. Be prepared.
o: Slow down and be ready to stop
Flash your lights to tell it to go
Sound your horn and keep going

q: Why is it harder to see motorcyclists at junctions?
e: Look carefully for motorcyclists — "think bike".
o: They are smaller and can be hidden by other vehicles or the windscreen pillar
They always ride in the middle of the road

q: When driving in town, what should you look for in shop windows and reflections?
e: Reflections can show hazards around corners.
o: Moving people or vehicles you can't see directly

q: You are driving towards a zebra crossing and a person with a white stick is waiting. What should you do?
e: A white stick means the person is blind or partially sighted.
o: Slow down and be ready to stop
Sound your horn to let them know you are there

q: What should you do when approaching traffic lights that have been green for some time?
e: Stale green lights may change to amber soon.
o: Be ready to stop, as they may change
Keep the same speed no matter what

q: You are driving behind a cyclist on a narrow road. A lorry is coming the other way. What should you do?
e: Don't overtake unless you can give the cyclist at least 1.5 metres at up to 30 mph.
o: Hold back until there is room to overtake safely
Sound your horn so the cyclist moves over
Overtake quickly before the lorry arrives

q: You are driving on a country road. What hazards should you expect?
e: Country roads may have no pavements, sharp bends and slow vehicles.
o: Animals, farm vehicles, horse riders and pedestrians walking in the road

q: Why should you slow down when passing a lorry that is reversing?
e: Large vehicles have big blind spots.
o: It may not be able to see you
It always needs the whole road

q: Which of these will most affect your ability to spot hazards?
e: Tiredness slows your reactions and reduces concentration.

q: Some cold and hay fever medicines can make you drowsy and affect your driving.
e: True — check the label or ask a pharmacist or doctor.

q: What is the drink-drive limit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
e: The limit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is 80 mg per 100 ml of blood (35 mcg per 100 ml of breath).
o: 80 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood

q: What is the drink-drive limit in Scotland?
e: Scotland's limit is lower: 50 mg per 100 ml of blood (22 mcg per 100 ml of breath).
o: 50 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood

q: What is the safest amount of alcohol to drink before driving?
e: The safest option is not to drink alcohol at all if you plan to drive.
o: Two drinks if you eat food

q: Alcohol can still be in your body the morning after drinking.
e: True — you may still be over the limit the next morning.

q: How does alcohol affect your driving?
e: Even small amounts can affect your driving.
o: It slows your reactions and affects your judgement
It has no effect if you feel fine

q: It is illegal to drive with certain drugs in your body above specified limits, including some prescription medicines.
e: True — and it's illegal to drive if any drug (legal or illegal) impairs your driving.

q: You are driving at night. What makes it harder to see pedestrians and cyclists?
e: Watch carefully for people in dark clothes, especially in rain.
o: Dark clothing and poor street lighting

q: A vehicle ahead is signalling left but is slowing down early. What might it be doing?
e: Signals can be misleading. Wait to see what the driver actually does.
o: Stopping or turning into a driveway before the junction

q: You see a red flashing light at a level crossing. What must you do?
e: You MUST stop when the red lights flash.
o: Speed up to cross before the train

q: You see road works ahead. What should you do?
e: Workers may be close to traffic. Temporary limits are there to protect them and you.
o: Obey the signs and speed limits and drive carefully

q: Why should you be careful when passing a stationary bus with its hazard lights on?
e: Slow down and be ready to stop.
o: Children or other passengers may be getting off and crossing
The driver may be on a break

q: You are about to drive home and feel very tired. What should you do?
e: Tiredness causes many serious crashes.
o: Don't drive until you have rested
Drink a lot of water and drive
Drive faster to get home sooner

q: You are on a road with a bend ahead and a cyclist in front. What is the safest thing to do?
e: Never overtake where you can't see far enough ahead.
o: Wait until after the bend when you can see the road is clear

q: A car in front suddenly brakes. What does keeping a safe gap give you?
e: A good gap gives you time and space to react.
o: Time to react and stop safely
A better view of the sky

q: Under the Highway Code's "hierarchy of road users", who has the greatest responsibility to reduce danger?
e: Drivers of larger and heavier vehicles have the greatest responsibility to look out for others.
o: Those driving vehicles that can cause the greatest harm

q: You are turning into a side road. A pedestrian is waiting to cross it. What should you do?
e: Since 2022, you should give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross a road you are turning into.

q: How much space should you leave when overtaking a cyclist at speeds up to 30 mph?
e: Leave at least 1.5 metres at up to 30 mph, and more at higher speeds.

q: How should you pass a horse rider?

q: How much space should you leave when passing a pedestrian walking in the road?

q: What does a pedestrian with a white stick with a red band mean?
e: A white stick with a red band means the person is deafblind.

e: A white stick shows the person is blind or partially sighted.

q: Which road users are most at risk on the road?

q: Why might a cyclist ride in the middle of a lane?

q: You are waiting to turn left. A cyclist is coming up on your left. What should you do?

q: A cycle lane is marked with a solid white line. What does this mean?

q: What is a toucan crossing?

q: What is an equestrian (Pegasus) crossing for?

q: You see older pedestrians starting to cross the road. What should you do?

q: Why should you take extra care near powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters?

q: What should you do when passing animals on the road?

Drive close to get past quickly

q: Why are motorcyclists vulnerable?

q: You are following a learner driver who stalls. What should you do?
e: Learners may be nervous. Give them time.

q: Where are you most likely to find young children crossing the road?

q: A pedestrian is already crossing a side road you want to turn into. What must you do?

q: Cyclists may ride two abreast. When should they ride in single file?

q: You are driving near a school with yellow zigzag lines outside. What does this mean?

q: What should you do if you are behind a snowplough or gritter?

It is the law to stop

e: Be ready to stop at the crossing.
o: Level crossing with a barrier or gate ahead

q: What does this sign mean?
e: Take extra care at crossings without barriers.
o: Level crossing without a barrier or gate ahead

q: What does this sign mean?
e: Your view ahead is limited — slow down.

q: What does this sign mean?
e: Use a low gear to control your speed.

q: What does this sign mean?
e: An exclamation mark warns of a hazard not covered by other signs.
o: Other danger — a plate below will say what

q: What does this sign mean?
e: Obey temporary limits and take care.
o: Men at work in the field

q: What colour are motorway direction signs, like this one?
e: Motorway signs are blue with white writing.

q: What does a green direction sign show?
e: Primary routes (main A roads) have green signs.

q: What does a white direction sign with black writing show?
e: Local routes have white signs with black writing.
o: Directions on non-primary and local roads

q: What does a brown sign show?
e: Brown signs point to tourist and leisure attractions.

q: What do yellow signs with black writing usually show?
e: Yellow signs are often used for diversions and events.

q: What do these markers show?
e: Each bar is about 100 yards on a motorway.
o: The distance to the next exit or junction

q: What does a red X over your lane mean?
e: A red X means the lane is closed.
o: Do not continue in that lane

q: What does this sign mean?
e: A white P on blue means a parking place.

q: What does this sign mean?
e: This rectangular sign tells you it's a one-way street.

q: What does this sign mean?
e: An H with a red cross on blue shows a hospital with A&E.
o: Hospital ahead with accident and emergency

q: What does a single white line across your lane at a junction mean?
e: A solid white line is a stop line.
o: Stop line — you must stop at it if there is a STOP sign or lights

q: What do white zigzag lines at a pedestrian crossing mean?
e: You MUST NOT park on them or overtake the leading vehicle.
o: No parking or overtaking the leading vehicle

q: What does a long white line with short gaps along the centre of the road mean?
e: Longer lines with short gaps warn of a hazard. Don't cross unless you can see the road is clear well ahead.
o: A hazard warning line — there is a hazard ahead

q: What do diagonal white stripes (hatching) in the middle of the road surrounded by a solid white line mean?
e: If the hatching is bordered by solid white lines, you MUST NOT enter it except in an emergency.
o: You must not enter except in an emergency

q: What does the word "SLOW" painted on the road mean?
e: There may be a hazard ahead.

q: What is the shape of the GIVE WAY sign?
e: Its unique shape helps you spot it.

q: What does a speed limit sign in a red circle on a gantry over the motorway mean?
e: Speed limits in a red ring are legal limits.
o: A compulsory limit you must not exceed

q: What is a "variable message sign" on a motorway for?
e: Always check overhead signs and signals.
o: To warn of hazards, delays and changes in speed limits

q: Before you can drive on the road as a learner, what must you have?
e: Learners need a provisional licence, insurance, L plates (or D plates in Wales) and a supervisor.
o: A provisional driving licence, insurance cover and a qualified supervisor

q: Who can supervise a learner driver?
e: Supervisors must be at least 21 and have held a full licence for at least 3 years.
o: Someone aged at least 21 who has held a full licence for that type of vehicle for at least 3 years

q: What plates must a learner driver display?
e: L or D plates must be clearly visible at the front and back.
o: L plates (or D plates in Wales) on the front and back
L plates on the back only

q: P plates (for new drivers) are compulsory.
e: False — P plates are optional, but they can let others know you've just passed.

q: What is the minimum insurance cover you need by law?
e: Third party cover pays for damage or injury to others.

q: What does "third party only" insurance cover?
e: It doesn't cover damage to your own car.
o: Damage or injury to other people and their property

q: What does fully comprehensive insurance usually cover?
e: It covers more, but costs more.
o: Damage to your own car as well as to other people and their property

q: When does a car first need an MOT certificate in England, Scotland and Wales?
e: After that, every year. (In Northern Ireland, the first MOT is at 4 years.)

q: What is a V5C?
e: It shows the registered keeper of the vehicle.

q: You change your address. Who must you tell?
e: Keep your licence and vehicle details up to date.
o: DVLA, so they can update your driving licence and V5C

q: What is a SORN?
e: If you take a vehicle off the road, you must make a SORN.
o: A Statutory Off Road Notification, telling DVLA a vehicle is not being used on the road

q: You must tax your vehicle even if it has a zero rate of tax.
e: True — you must still tax it, even if you pay nothing.

q: The police ask to see your documents and you don't have them with you. What can happen?
e: You may be asked to produce your licence, insurance and MOT within 7 days.
o: You can be asked to take them to a police station within 7 days

q: What happens if a new driver gets 6 or more penalty points within 2 years of passing their test?
e: Under the New Drivers Act, 6 points within 2 years means losing your licence and retaking your tests.
o: Their licence is revoked and they must reapply for a provisional licence

q: What is the penalty for driving without insurance?
e: Courts can give unlimited fines and disqualification.
o: Usually a £300 fine and 6 penalty points, and it can go to court

q: How long is a full car driving licence photocard valid before you need to renew it?
e: The photocard must be renewed every 10 years. Your entitlement lasts until 70, then you renew every 3 years.

q: What age can you usually start driving a car on the road with a provisional licence?
e: You can apply for a provisional licence at 15 years 9 months and drive a car at 17.

q: What happens to your licence at age 70?
e: Renewal is free at 70 and every 3 years after.
o: You must renew it, then every 3 years
You must take a test again

q: Who is responsible for making sure a vehicle is roadworthy and has a valid MOT?
e: The driver is responsible for the vehicle they drive.

q: You arrive first at a crash. What should you do first?
e: Check for danger first. Then call 999 or 112.
o: Warn other traffic, for example with hazard warning lights, and make sure you are safe
Move the injured people straight away

q: Which emergency numbers can you call in the UK?
e: 999 and 112 both work in the UK.

q: What should you NOT do for injured people at a crash scene?
e: Don't move casualties unless there's further danger, such as fire.
o: Move them, unless they are in danger

q: An injured motorcyclist is lying in the road. What should you do about their helmet?
e: Removing a helmet could cause more injury.
o: Leave it on unless it's essential to remove it, for example if they aren't breathing
Take it off to give them a drink

q: What does "DR ABC" stand for in first aid?
e: Check for danger, response, open the airway, check breathing, and start compressions if needed.

q: A casualty is not breathing normally. What should you do?
e: Push firmly in the centre of the chest, 5–6 cm deep, at a rate of 100–120 per minute.
o: Wait for help without doing anything

q: How deep should you press when giving chest compressions to an adult?
e: Press firmly and quickly, 100–120 times a minute.

q: Someone is bleeding heavily from a wound. What should you do?
e: Firm pressure helps stop bleeding.
o: Press firmly on the wound with something clean

q: How should you treat a burn at a crash scene?
e: Don't remove anything stuck to the burn.
o: Cool it with clean, cold water or other non-toxic liquid for at least 10 minutes
Remove clothing stuck to the skin

q: Why should you not give an injured person anything to eat or drink?
e: Keep them warm and calm instead.

q: How far behind your vehicle should you place a warning triangle on a normal road?
e: Don't use warning triangles on motorways.

q: You are involved in a collision where someone is injured. What must you do?
e: If someone is injured, you must also show your insurance certificate or produce it to the police within 7 days.
o: Stop, and give your details — or report it to the police as soon as possible, within 24 hours
Wait a week and then report it

q: You hit a parked car and can't find the owner. What must you do?
e: You MUST report it to the police if you can't give your details to the owner.
o: Report it to the police as soon as possible, within 24 hours

q: Your vehicle catches fire while driving. What should you do?
e: Get well clear. Don't open the bonnet if the fire is in the engine compartment.
o: Pull over, switch off the engine, get everyone out and call 999
Try to put it out by opening the bonnet wide

q: What should you do if you break down on an ordinary road?
e: Use your hazard warning lights, and a warning triangle if safe.
o: Get your vehicle off the road if possible and use hazard lights
Stay in the middle of the road
Open the bonnet and sit in the car
Walk off and leave the car

q: You see a crash on the other side of a motorway. What should you do?
e: "Rubbernecking" causes more crashes.
o: Keep going and concentrate on your own driving
Stop on the hard shoulder to help

q: In a tunnel, your vehicle breaks down. What should you do?
e: Follow the instructions and use the emergency points.
o: Switch on hazard lights, switch off the engine and use the emergency phone
Stay in the car with the engine running

q: A tyre bursts while you are driving. What should you do?
e: Keep control and stop gradually at a safe place.
o: Hold the steering wheel firmly and slow down gradually

q: Who should you tell if you see dangerous items fall from a vehicle on a motorway?
e: Never try to remove things from a motorway yourself.
o: The police or National Highways, using an emergency phone or calling from a safe place

q: At a crash, what does a vehicle displaying an orange hazard warning plate mean?
e: Give the details on the plate to the emergency services.
o: It may be carrying dangerous goods — keep well back and tell the emergency services

q: What is the recovery position for?
e: Only move a casualty if there's danger, or if they're breathing but unconscious and need their airway kept clear.
o: Keeping an unconscious person who is breathing in a safe position so their airway stays open
Moving a person to your car

q: Who is responsible for making sure a vehicle is not overloaded?
e: You MUST NOT overload your vehicle or trailer.

q: How does a heavy load on a roof rack affect your car?
e: Weight high up changes handling.
o: It makes the car less stable, especially on bends and in wind

q: You are carrying a heavy load. What may you need to adjust?
e: Check your handbook for the right tyre pressures and headlight settings for heavy loads.

q: Why must loads be secured?
e: An unsecured load is dangerous to you and others.
o: So they don't fall off or move and make the vehicle unstable

q: What should you fit to help stop a caravan snaking?
e: A stabiliser can help, but it won't stop snaking if the load is wrong.

q: Your caravan starts to snake. What should you do?
e: Slow down gently until it is under control.
o: Ease off the accelerator and slow down gradually

q: How should you load a caravan or trailer?
e: This keeps the caravan stable.
o: Heavy items low down and near the axle

q: When towing, what extra mirrors may you need?
e: You must have a clear view behind.
o: Towing mirrors, so you can see past the caravan or trailer

q: Where can you find the maximum weight your car can tow?
e: Don't exceed the limits set by the manufacturer.
o: In the vehicle handbook or on the vehicle's VIN plate

q: What should you do if a roof rack is no longer needed?
e: Roof racks add drag and use more fuel.
o: Remove it to reduce drag and save fuel

q: A dog is travelling in your car. How should it be carried?
e: Use a harness, cage or guard.
o: Suitably restrained so it can't distract you or be hurt
In the boot with the parcel shelf in place

q: Who must check that a child passenger is properly restrained?
e: The driver is legally responsible for children under 14.
